elements.name: Null Object
elements.what: An object with neutral do-nothing behavior that stands in for the absence of a real collaborator, conforming to the same interface.
elements.problem: Callers otherwise litter code with null checks before every use of an optional collaborator; a null object makes 'nothing there' a polymorphic case instead of a conditional.
elements.named_in: Null Object - Bobby Woolf, in Pattern Languages of Program Design 3 (1998; PLoP 1996)

elements.name: Sentinel Value
elements.what: A special in-band value, distinct from all legal data, used to signal a condition such as end-of-data, absence, or failure (NUL terminator, -1, null pointer).
elements.problem: When a channel or return type has no out-of-band way to signal termination or absence, a reserved value carries the signal without extra state or size bookkeeping.
elements.named_in: The Art of Computer Programming Vol. 3: Sorting and Searching - Donald Knuth (1973); also Code Complete 2nd ed. - McConnell (2004)

elements.name: Multiton
elements.what: A class that manages a map of named instances of itself, guaranteeing exactly one instance per key.
elements.problem: Singleton generalized: a system needs a controlled, globally accessible set of instances keyed by identity (one per database, one per device) rather than one total.
elements.named_in: Multiton pattern - Wikipedia (software design pattern list, creational)

elements.name: Lazy Initialization
elements.what: Defer creating an object or computing a value until its first use, typically guarded by a null/flag check or a holder construct.
elements.problem: Eager construction of expensive or rarely-used objects wastes startup time and memory; deferral pays the cost only when and if the value is needed.
elements.named_in: Lazy initialization - Wikipedia (software design pattern list, creational); discussed in GoF Singleton implementation

elements.name: Double Dispatch
elements.what: A technique where the operation executed depends on the runtime types of two receivers, implemented by a pair of single dispatches (each object virtual-calls into the other).
elements.problem: Single-dispatch languages select behavior on one receiver only; interactions like collide(shapeA, shapeB) or Visitor's element/visitor pairing need selection on two types.
elements.named_in: A Simple Technique for Handling Multiple Polymorphism - Daniel H. H. Ingalls (OOPSLA 1986); mechanism underlying GoF Visitor

elements.name: Twin
elements.what: Model multiple inheritance in a single-inheritance language by splitting one conceptual object into two closely coupled partner objects, each subclassing one parent and holding a reference to its twin.
elements.problem: Languages like Java forbid inheriting from two classes; the twin pair simulates the combined subtype while avoiding the diamond problem.
elements.named_in: Twin - A Design Pattern for Modelling Multiple Inheritance - Hannes Moessenboeck (Johannes Kepler University Linz)

elements.name: Role Object
elements.what: Adapt a core object to different client contexts by attaching and detaching role objects at runtime, each role extending the core's interface for one context.
elements.problem: One domain object (Customer) is viewed differently by many subsystems; subclassing per view explodes and freezes the combination at compile time, while roles compose dynamically.
elements.named_in: The Role Object Pattern - Dirk Baeumer, Dirk Riehle, Wolf Siberski, Martina Wulf (PLoP 1997)

elements.name: Servant
elements.what: A helper class that provides a common behavior (e.g., movement, printing) to a group of otherwise unrelated classes, which are passed to the servant as parameters.
elements.problem: A behavior is needed by many classes that share no useful ancestor; centralizing it in a servant avoids duplicating the implementation in each class.
elements.named_in: Servant (design pattern) - Wikipedia (software design pattern list, behavioral)
elements.borderline: Thin catalog presence outside Wikipedia; mechanism overlaps plain utility/strategy composition - included per charter with the honest tag.

elements.name: Event Aggregator
elements.what: A single object that channels events from many sources to many subscribers, so producers and consumers register only with the aggregator.
elements.problem: With many event sources, direct Observer wiring forces every consumer to know and subscribe to every source; the aggregator collapses the many-to-many registration into one point.
elements.named_in: Event Aggregator - Martin Fowler, Further Enterprise Application Architecture development (eaaDev, 2004)

elements.name: Dependency Injection
elements.what: An assembler supplies a component's dependencies from outside (via constructor, setter, or interface) instead of the component constructing or locating them itself.
elements.problem: Components that instantiate their own collaborators are hard-wired to concrete classes, untestable in isolation, and unconfigurable; injection moves the wiring decision out of the component.
elements.named_in: Inversion of Control Containers and the Dependency Injection pattern - Martin Fowler (2004)

elements.name: Service Locator
elements.what: A well-known registry object that components query at runtime to obtain their dependencies by name or type.
elements.problem: Components need configurable access to services without hard-coding concrete classes; the locator centralizes lookup, at the cost of a hidden dependency on the locator itself.
elements.named_in: Core J2EE Patterns - Deepak Alur, John Crupi, Dan Malks (2001); analyzed vs DI in Fowler (2004)

elements.name: Callback
elements.what: A piece of executable code (function pointer, closure, object method) passed to another component to be invoked later at a defined point, synchronously or asynchronously.
elements.problem: A library or lower layer must trigger caller-defined behavior without compile-time knowledge of it; passing the code in inverts control while keeping the layers decoupled.
elements.named_in: Callback (computer programming) - Wikipedia
elements.borderline: Fundamental technique near the syntax floor, but named, recurring, and the basis of whole API styles - included.

elements.name: Hook Method
elements.what: A method deliberately left empty or with default behavior at a designed extension point, which subclasses or clients override to inject custom behavior into a fixed skeleton.
elements.problem: Frameworks and template algorithms need designated points of planned variability; hooks let extenders customize behavior without touching the invariant control flow.
elements.named_in: Meta Patterns - A Means for Capturing the Essentials of Reusable Object-Oriented Design - Wolfgang Pree (ECOOP 1994); 'hook operations' in GoF Template Method
elements.borderline: Fold-vs-separate decision: kept separate from Template Method because hook methods recur outside it (framework hot spots, lifecycle hooks, event hooks); logged per charter.

elements.name: Cache-Aside
elements.what: Application code checks the cache first, loads from the backing store on miss, populates the cache, and invalidates or updates the entry on writes.
elements.problem: When the cache is not transparent (no read-through support), the application itself must keep cache and store coherent while still gaining read-latency benefits.
elements.named_in: Cloud Design Patterns - Microsoft Azure Architecture Center

elements.name: Humble Object
elements.what: Strip hard-to-test code (GUI bindings, thread glue, framework touchpoints) down to a trivial 'humble' shell that immediately delegates all logic to a testable collaborator.
elements.problem: Logic embedded in untestable contexts (event handlers, ISRs, UI classes) cannot be unit-tested; extracting it leaves only trivially-correct glue untested.
elements.named_in: xUnit Test Patterns: Refactoring Test Code - Gerard Meszaros (2007)
elements.borderline: Testability-driven structuring pattern; passes altitude as a concrete code-level construct, not a process practice.

elements.name: Test Double
elements.what: A substitute object installed in place of a production dependency during a test; the family spans dummy, fake, stub, spy, and mock by increasing behavioral sophistication.
elements.problem: Real dependencies make tests slow, nondeterministic, or unable to observe indirect inputs/outputs; a double controls the collaborator's behavior and records interactions.
elements.named_in: xUnit Test Patterns: Refactoring Test Code - Gerard Meszaros (2007)
elements.borderline: Folded mock/stub/fake/spy/dummy into one element per charter; kept IN as a code construct (a class you write), not a process practice.

elements.name: Object Mother
elements.what: A factory class dedicated to producing ready-made, semantically meaningful example objects (a standard customer, an overdue invoice) for use across many tests.
elements.problem: Complex domain objects are tedious to assemble in every test; a shared mother centralizes canonical test fixtures, at the cost of coupling tests to shared exemplars.
elements.named_in: ObjectMother: Easing Test Object Creation in XP - Peter Schuh, Stephanie Punke (XP Universe 2001); name coined on a ThoughtWorks project
elements.borderline: Test-support construction class; code-level construct in the testing domain.

elements.name: Test Data Builder
elements.what: A builder with sensible defaults and fluent with-methods used in tests to construct complex objects, overriding only the fields relevant to each test.
elements.problem: Object Mothers proliferate variants and obscure which attributes matter to a test; a builder makes the significant values explicit while defaulting the rest.
elements.named_in: Test Data Builders: an alternative to the Object Mother pattern - Nat Pryce (2007); also in Growing Object-Oriented Software, Guided by Tests - Freeman & Pryce (2009)
elements.borderline: Test-support construction class; distinct mechanism from Object Mother (parameterized builder vs canned factory), so two entries.

elements.name: Delegation
elements.what: An object handles a request by forwarding it to a helper object (the delegate), optionally passing itself so the delegate can refer back to the original receiver.
elements.problem: Behavior reuse without inheritance: composition plus forwarding lets behavior be chosen and changed at runtime and shared across unrelated classes.
elements.named_in: Using Prototypical Objects to Implement Shared Behavior in Object-Oriented Systems - Henry Lieberman (OOPSLA 1986); discussed as a reuse mechanism in GoF
elements.borderline: Fundamental technique rather than a discrete pattern; included because it is named, recurring, and catalogued (Wikipedia structural list, GoF).

elements.name: Marker Interface
elements.what: An empty interface implemented solely to attach a type-level property to a class (java.io.Serializable), checkable at compile time or via runtime type tests.
elements.problem: Metadata about a class must be expressible in the type system itself so that APIs can require or detect the property; markers do this without annotations or fields.
elements.named_in: Effective Java - Joshua Bloch (2001)

elements.name: Specification
elements.what: Encapsulate a business rule as a first-class predicate object with an isSatisfiedBy(candidate) method, composable via and/or/not into richer rules.
elements.problem: Selection, validation, and construction-to-order criteria otherwise scatter as ad hoc conditionals; reified specifications make rules combinable, testable, and reusable.
elements.named_in: Specifications - Eric Evans, Martin Fowler (PLoP 1997 workshop paper)

elements.name: Private Class Data
elements.what: Move a class's state into a separate data object initialized once at construction, exposing it to the main class only through read access.
elements.problem: Write access to fields after construction invites unintended mutation; separating the data class enforces initialize-then-read-only discipline structurally.
elements.named_in: Private Class Data - SourceMaking design patterns catalog (structural)

elements.name: Monostate
elements.what: A class whose every instance shares the same state by declaring all fields static, so construction is unrestricted but behavior is singleton-like.
elements.problem: Singleton's single-instance enforcement leaks into client code; Monostate gives shared-state semantics behind an ordinary class interface, swappable and subclassable.
elements.named_in: Agile Software Development: Principles, Patterns, and Practices - Robert C. Martin (2002); originally Ball & Crawford

elements.name: Fluent Interface
elements.what: An API designed as an internal DSL where methods return context objects so calls chain into readable, sentence-like configuration or construction sequences.
elements.problem: Multi-step configuration through setters or telescoping constructors reads poorly and invites invalid intermediate states; fluent design optimizes the call-site for readability.
elements.named_in: FluentInterface - Martin Fowler (bliki, 2005, with Eric Evans)

elements.name: Extension Object
elements.what: Let clients ask an object for an extension implementing a specific interface (getExtension(type)), so new interfaces can be added to a class family without changing its core.
elements.problem: Unanticipated clients need new operations on existing abstractions; extensions attach role-specific interfaces without bloating the base class or breaking existing clients.
elements.named_in: Extension Object - Erich Gamma, in Pattern Languages of Program Design 3 (1998)

elements.name: Type Object
elements.what: Represent a class-like concept as a runtime object: instances hold a reference to a shared type object that carries the data and behavior common to their 'kind'.
elements.problem: When the set of kinds (monster species, document types) must grow without recompiling, hard-coded subclasses fail; type objects make kinds data-driven at runtime.
elements.named_in: The Type Object Pattern - Ralph Johnson, Bobby Woolf, in Pattern Languages of Program Design 3 (1998); modern treatment in Game Programming Patterns - Nystrom (2014)

elements.name: Acyclic Visitor
elements.what: A Visitor variant that breaks the dependency cycle between the element hierarchy and the visitor by using a degenerate base visitor plus per-element visitor interfaces and a runtime cast.
elements.problem: Classic GoF Visitor couples every visitor to every element class, forcing full recompilation when elements change; the acyclic form allows partial visitors and incremental growth.
elements.named_in: Acyclic Visitor - Robert C. Martin, in Pattern Languages of Program Design 3 (1998)

elements.name: Serializer
elements.what: Stream objects into and out of arbitrary backends by pairing a Reader/Writer protocol with backend-specific concrete serializers, keeping the object graph traversal generic.
elements.problem: Objects must move across formats and media (files, network, databases) without embedding format knowledge in every class; the pattern isolates format behind a uniform protocol.
elements.named_in: Serializer - Dirk Riehle, Wolf Siberski, Dirk Baeumer, Daniel Megert, Heinz Zuellighoven, in Pattern Languages of Program Design 3 (1998)

elements.name: Object Pool
elements.what: Recycle a bounded set of pre-allocated objects: clients acquire an instance from the pool, use it, and release it back rather than constructing and destroying.
elements.problem: Expensive or allocation-averse objects (connections, buffers, threads; embedded no-heap contexts) make per-use construction unacceptable; pooling amortizes and bounds the cost.
elements.named_in: Pooling - in Pattern-Oriented Software Architecture Vol. 3: Patterns for Resource Management - Kircher, Jain (2004)

elements.name: Module Pattern
elements.what: Use a closure (classically an IIFE) to create private state and functions, returning an object that exposes only the intended public interface.
elements.problem: Languages without native access modifiers or namespaces (pre-ES6 JavaScript) need encapsulation and a single namespace-safe export; the closure provides both.
elements.named_in: Learning JavaScript Design Patterns - Addy Osmani (2012); popularized by Crockford

elements.name: Guard Clause
elements.what: Check for special or invalid cases at the top of a routine and return/throw immediately, keeping the main path unindented and free of nested conditionals.
elements.problem: Deeply nested if/else for edge cases obscures the dominant logic; guards state preconditions explicitly and exit early.
elements.named_in: Refactoring: Improving the Design of Existing Code - Martin Fowler (1999), 'Replace Nested Conditional with Guard Clauses'
elements.borderline: Small-scale idiom near the raw-syntax floor; included as a named, recurring, catalogued construct.

elements.name: Collecting Parameter
elements.what: Pass a collecting object through a series of methods, each of which adds its partial results to it, instead of composing return values.
elements.problem: Building a compound result (a report, an aggregate collection) across many methods via return values forces awkward merging; a shared collector accumulates in place.
elements.named_in: Smalltalk Best Practice Patterns - Kent Beck (1997)
elements.borderline: Micro-scale code-organization pattern; included because it is named in a canonical catalog and recurs across codebases.

elements.name: Circuit Breaker
elements.what: A stateful proxy around a failure-prone operation that trips open after repeated failures, fails fast while open, and probes (half-open) before closing again.
elements.problem: Retrying a dependency that is down burns resources and cascades failure; the breaker converts hammering into fast failure and controlled recovery probing.
elements.named_in: Release It!: Design and Deploy Production-Ready Software - Michael T. Nygard (2007); also Azure Cloud Design Patterns

elements.name: Bulkhead
elements.what: Partition resources (thread pools, connection pools, queues) into isolated compartments per client or workload so exhaustion or failure in one compartment cannot sink the rest.
elements.problem: A single shared pool lets one misbehaving consumer starve all others; compartmentalization contains the damage, trading peak utilization for isolation.
elements.named_in: Release It!: Design and Deploy Production-Ready Software - Michael T. Nygard (2007); also Azure Cloud Design Patterns
elements.borderline: Also an infrastructure/deployment tactic; the in-process form (partitioned pools) passes the altitude test and is what is catalogued here.

elements.name: Immutable Object
elements.what: An object whose observable state cannot change after construction; all 'modifications' produce new instances.
elements.problem: Shared mutable state requires defensive copying and synchronization; immutability makes objects freely shareable, cacheable, and inherently thread-safe.
elements.named_in: Immutable - Mark Grand, Patterns in Java Vol. 1 (1998); reinforced in Effective Java - Bloch (2001) and Java Concurrency in Practice - Goetz et al. (2006)

elements.name: Notification
elements.what: An object that accumulates errors and messages during an operation (typically validation) and is returned or passed across a layer boundary instead of throwing on first failure.
elements.problem: Exceptions abort at the first problem and cross layer boundaries poorly; a notification gathers all failures so callers can report them together.
elements.named_in: Notification - Martin Fowler, Further Enterprise Application Architecture development (eaaDev)

elements.name: Memoization
elements.what: Cache the results of a (pure) function keyed by its arguments so repeated calls with the same inputs return the stored result instead of recomputing.
elements.problem: Expensive deterministic computations invoked repeatedly with recurring arguments waste time; trading memory for lookup eliminates the recomputation.
elements.named_in: Memo functions and machine learning - Donald Michie (Nature, 1968)

parked_architecture.name: Sidecar
parked_architecture.why: Azure: auxiliary component deployed as a separate process/container alongside the main application - deployment topology.

parked_architecture.name: Ambassador
parked_architecture.why: Azure: out-of-process helper proxy for remote communication on behalf of a service - topology.

parked_architecture.name: Gateway Aggregation / Gateway Routing / Gateway Offloading
parked_architecture.why: Azure: system-edge gateway structures - topology.

parked_architecture.name: Backends for Frontends
parked_architecture.why: Azure: per-frontend backend services - whole-system structuring.

parked_architecture.name: Gatekeeper
parked_architecture.why: Azure: dedicated validating host between clients and backends - deployment topology for security.

parked_architecture.name: Anti-Corruption Layer
parked_architecture.why: Azure/DDD: translation layer between systems/bounded contexts - inter-system structure.

parked_architecture.name: Strangler Fig
parked_architecture.why: Azure/Fowler: incremental legacy-system replacement strategy - system migration structure.

parked_architecture.name: Queue-Based Load Leveling
parked_architecture.why: Azure: queue as buffer between services - inter-service topology (in-process message queue is a separate design element owned elsewhere).

parked_architecture.name: Competing Consumers
parked_architecture.why: Azure/EIP: multiple consumer instances on a shared channel - system-scale messaging.

parked_architecture.name: Publisher-Subscriber
parked_architecture.why: Azure: system-scale async messaging topology; in-process pub-sub is covered by Observer/Event Aggregator in the design realm.

parked_architecture.name: CQRS
parked_architecture.why: Azure: separate read/write models across a system - data-architecture style.

parked_architecture.name: Event Sourcing
parked_architecture.why: Azure: append-only event store as the system of record - data-architecture level (db scout may claim a mechanism-level form).

parked_architecture.name: Saga / Compensating Transaction
parked_architecture.why: Azure: distributed transaction coordination across services.

parked_architecture.name: Scheduler Agent Supervisor
parked_architecture.why: Azure: distributed action coordination and recovery - multi-service structure.

parked_architecture.name: Leader Election
parked_architecture.why: Azure: coordination across distributed instances - distributed-systems mechanism above component level.

parked_architecture.name: Sharding
parked_architecture.why: Azure: horizontal partitioning of a data store - data-architecture.

parked_architecture.name: Deployment Stamps / Geode
parked_architecture.why: Azure: replicated deployment units / geo-distributed nodes - deployment topology.

parked_architecture.name: Federated Identity / Valet Key
parked_architecture.why: Azure: cross-system authentication delegation / token-based direct resource access - system-level security structures.

parked_architecture.name: Health Endpoint Monitoring
parked_architecture.why: Azure: externally-probed health checks - operational/system monitoring structure.

parked_architecture.name: Static Content Hosting / External Configuration Store
parked_architecture.why: Azure: moving content/config to external services - deployment decisions.

parked_architecture.name: Claim Check / Sequential Convoy / Messaging Bridge / Asynchronous Request-Reply / Choreography
parked_architecture.why: Azure/EIP system-messaging patterns - inter-service; EIP scout may claim mid-level subsets.

parked_architecture.name: Compute Resource Consolidation
parked_architecture.why: Azure: packing tasks into deployment units - deployment-level.

parked_architecture.name: Index Table / Materialized View
parked_architecture.why: Azure: data-tier query structures - data-architecture; db scout may claim mechanism-level forms.

parked_architecture.name: Blackboard
parked_architecture.why: On Wikipedia's behavioral list but canonically a POSA1 architectural pattern - system-level knowledge-source structure.

parked_architecture.name: Front Controller
parked_architecture.why: On Wikipedia's structural list; PoEAA web-app request-handling structure - upward-borderline, poeaa scout overlap.

parked_architecture.name: Half-Object + Protocol (HOPP)
parked_architecture.why: PLoP (Meszaros 1995): splitting an object across address spaces with a protocol between halves - distribution structure.

excluded_notable.name: Anti-patterns (God Object, Big Ball of Mud, Poltergeist, magic numbers, cloud antipattern catalog)
excluded_notable.why: Charter rule: anti-patterns are not elements; Azure maintains a separate antipatterns catalog.

excluded_notable.name: Inversion of Control
excluded_notable.why: Principle, not a mechanism; realized by concrete elements (dependency injection, hook methods, callbacks).

excluded_notable.name: xUnit test-organization patterns (Four-Phase Test, Fresh Fixture, Testcase Class per Class, etc.)
excluded_notable.why: Meszaros patterns about test structure/process, not code-level constructs; only the code-construct subset (Test Double, Humble Object) taken.

excluded_notable.name: Composed Method (Beck)
excluded_notable.why: Code-style/refactoring guidance at raw-code altitude, not a reusable mechanism.

excluded_notable.name: Quarantine (Azure)
excluded_notable.why: Supply-chain/ops practice, not an implementable mechanism.

excluded_notable.name: Design principles (SOLID, Law of Demeter, DRY)

notes: Coverage: swept Wikipedia software-design-pattern list (live), Azure Cloud Design Patterns catalog (live, full table triaged in-process vs parked), SourceMaking (live), Fowler eaaDev + bliki (live: Event Aggregator, Notification, TestDouble coinage, ObjectMother attribution), PLoPD3 classics from deep familiarity (Null Object, Extension Object, Type Object, Acyclic Visitor, Serializer, Role Object). xunitpatterns.com was unreachable this session (ECONNREFUSED twice); Meszaros items confirmed via Fowler's TestDouble bliki instead. Decisions logged: hook method kept SEPARATE from Template Method (recurs outside it); Test Double folded to one element per charter; Object Mother and Test Data Builder kept as TWO elements (canned factory vs parameterized builder - different mechanisms); initialization-on-demand holder folded into lazy-initialization aka; method chaining folded into fluent-interface aka; Special Case folded into null-object aka (poeaa scout may prefer to split). Deliberate overlaps left to sibling scouts (dedup at merge): cache-aside/circuit-breaker (db/error scouts), object-pool (resource scout, posa3), specification (poeaa scout), retry/throttling/rate-limiting (error/robustness scouts - NOT enumerated here though Azure names them). Wikipedia concurrency-table entries (Balking, Guarded Suspension, Binding Properties, Scheduler, Thread-Specific Storage, Double-Checked Locking) deliberately left to the concurrency scout. Thin spots: Fowler eaaDev UI patterns (Presentation Model, Passive View, Supervising Controller) and c2-wiki Smalltalk micro-patterns (Pluggable Selector, Method Object) claimed by no scout as far as visible - flag for gap hunt; c2 wiki itself not fetched live (names cross-confirmed via other catalogs).
